 What 10GbE asks of the rest of the system
 The network is only as fast as its slowest link, so 10GbE on the NAS needs a 10GbE switch port and a 10GbE port on the computer, or a direct cable between the two.
 Hard drives are the next limit. Western Digital lists its 26TB drives at under 305MB a second sustained, and a 10GbE link carries about 1,250MB a second, so the port pays off with several drives in an array, or with SSDs.
 For a direct connection to one computer, the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro, UGREEN DXP8800 Plus and UGREEN DXP480T Plus also list two Thunderbolt 4 ports.

 2-Bay vs. 4-Bay Technical & Financial Comparison
 A factual breakdown of why bay count fundamentally changes storage math, expansion friction, and dollar-per-terabyte value.
 Storage Efficiency & Dollar-per-TB Economics
 2-Bay Architecture 50% capacity efficiency with a two-drive RAID 1 mirror
 4-Bay Architecture 75% capacity efficiency with four equal drives in RAID 5
 Evidence Note: Four equal drives in RAID 5 provide three drives worth of capacity; a two-drive mirror provides one. The cost per usable TB depends on exact enclosure and disk prices, so use the complete-build table.
 Expansion Strategy (Start with 3, Keep 1 Free)
 2-Bay Architecture No free bays; replace disks one at a time with a complete rebuild after each
 4-Bay Architecture Start with 3 drives; a supported fourth-drive expansion increases 24TB to 36TB (50%)
 Evidence Note: Three 12TB drives provide 24TB decimal capacity with single parity; four provide 36TB. Expansion requires a supported pool operation and time to complete. Back up first and allow for reduced performance.
 Dual-Parity Tolerance (RAID 6 / SHR-2)
 2-Bay Architecture Impossible (maximum 1 drive failure tolerance)
 4-Bay Architecture Supported (tolerates 2 simultaneous disk failures with 50% capacity)
 Evidence Note: RAID 6 can tolerate any two drive failures. It does not protect against every cause of data loss or enclosure failure, and rebuild time varies. Keep an independent backup and a recovery plan.
 Hardware Compute & Networking Headroom
 2-Bay Architecture Mainly entry CPUs (N100/J4125), single 1GbE/2.5GbE, 2–8GB RAM
 4-Bay Architecture High-end CPUs (Intel 8505/Ryzen V1500B), native 10GbE, PCIe slots, up to 64GB RAM

 Rules for Choosing a 4 -Bay NAS
 1 Start with 3 equal drives under SHR / RAID 5 to enjoy 1-drive parity while leaving 1 bay free for zero-downtime future expansion. 
 2 Use RAID 5 for media and backups to maximize capacity (75% usable). Choose RAID 6 / SHR-2 dual parity for irreplaceable business files. 
 3 If streaming 4K movies with subtitle transcoding, verify that the NAS processor features an Intel Quick Sync GPU. 
 4 Pair 4-bay systems with a compatible UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) to prevent array corruption during unexpected power outages. 
 Mistakes to Avoid Before Buying
 ✕ Filling all 4 bays on day 1 with small 2TB drives, eliminating easy expansion. 
 ✕ Choosing a non-iGPU processor (like AMD Ryzen V1500B) when intensive 4K Plex hardware transcoding is required. 
 ✕ Overlooking noise: 4 × 7200rpm drives can be audible in a bedroom; locate the NAS in an office or utility closet. 
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Why is a 4-bay NAS considered the best choice for home use?
 A 4-bay NAS hits the mathematical sweet spot: RAID 5 gives you 75% usable capacity (versus 50% in a 2-bay RAID 1 mirror), while providing full 1-disk failure protection. You can also populate 3 bays initially and preserve the 4th bay for hassle-free storage expansion.
 What is the cheapest 4-bay NAS in 2026?
 Enclosures like the TerraMaster F4-424 and UGREEN DXP4800 represent the most affordable modern 4-bay entry points with Intel processors, starting around $400 to $450 before hard drives.
 How much does a complete 4-bay NAS cost with hard drives?
 Use the exact-model cost table below the picks and compare both total spend and protected capacity. Three 12TB drives under single parity provide 24TB decimal capacity; four provide 36TB. Checkout prices, tax, shipping, backup storage, and network upgrades can change the final budget.
 Can I start a 4-bay NAS with just 2 hard drives?
 Some systems allow a two-drive mirror or SHR pool to grow by adding disks and migrating to single parity. The supported steps depend on the operating system and existing RAID layout; conversion is not automatic on every NAS. Read the model-specific procedure and verify your independent backup before changing the pool.
 What is the difference between RAID 5 and RAID 6 in a 4-bay NAS?
 RAID 5 allocates one drive worth of storage to parity (75% usable with 4 drives) and survives one disk failure. RAID 6 uses dual parity (50% usable with 4 drives) and survives two simultaneous drive crashes, which is recommended for mission-critical business retention or when rebuilding high-capacity 16TB+ arrays.

Plex is a media platform that stands out as the best option in this category; it's easy to set up and use, and it has a growing library of content. The best way to install and manage Plex is on a NAS server, and there are models that excel at this use case.
 I've been using NAS servers for well over a decade now, and I crossed 500TB of storage in my homelab across all storage servers. I tested all major 4-bay NAS models available at the moment, and UGREEN's DXP4800 Pro gets my vote. I tested the DXP4800 Pro a few weeks ago, and there's no doubt in my mind that this is the best 4-bay Plex NAS you can buy in 2026.
 The DXP4800 Pro launched at the end of last year for $699, and it got a price hike to $719 because of the RAM crisis. But right now, you can get it for $639 on Amazon during Prime Day , its lowest price yet and a decent $80 discount.

 In short, this is one of the best mainstream 4-bay NAS servers around today. The DXP4800 Pro is an outstanding Plex server, so if you're looking at a home NAS that's aimed at media streaming and hardware transcoding, I wouldn't consider any other model. It's also great as a hobbyist NAS, so if you're looking to run containers and build hobby projects, this is the one I'd get.
 The software was a big limitation when UGREEN made its debut in this category two years ago, but the brand made decent inroads, particularly over the last six months. You'll get all the basics around data storage, plugging into public cloud servers, photo and video organization, and advanced tools around virtualization. There's also the inherent advantage of being able to run TrueNAS or any other media server platform if you want additional flexibility.
 Basically, the DXP4800 Pro has everything you need in a 4-bay Plex NAS, and with the deal bringing it down to $639 , this is the best time to get the server.

 10GbE SSD NAS Under $500 in 2026: Which Models Actually Qualify?
 Release date:
 Jul 22,2026
 In this article
 Share this article 
 A sub-$500 NAS with true 10GbE and an SSD-based storage pool sounds easy to find. In practice, the list is surprisingly short. 
 Many products shown in searches for “budget 10GbE NAS” use 5GbE, combine two 2.5GbE ports, rely primarily on hard drives, or only fall below $500 during a limited promotion. Those systems may still be good choices, but they do not all meet the same requirement. 
 For this guide, a NAS must pass three checks: 
 It has a true 10GbE network connection. 
 It can use SSDs as the main storage pool, not only as a cache. 
 Its normal diskless price is below $500 in the United States. 
 Based on the widely available products we could verify, the LincStation N2 is the clearest match. A few other models come close, but miss the price, network, or storage requirement. 
 What counts as a 10GbE SSD NAS? 
 1. A true 10GbE connection 
 A qualifying system needs a single 10GbE link, either through 10GBASE-T RJ45 or SFP+. 
 A 5GbE port does not qualify. Two 2.5GbE ports also do not provide a single 5Gbps or 10Gbps transfer by default. Link aggregation can distribute separate network sessions across multiple ports, but one file transfer is normally limited by the speed of one connection. 
 That distinction matters for people editing large files directly from a NAS or moving large project folders during the working day. 
 2. SSDs as primary storage 
 An SSD NAS should be able to store the main data pool on solid-state drives. 
 A conventional four-bay hard-drive NAS with two M.2 cache slots is not the same thing. Cache can improve frequently accessed data, application loading, and metadata work, but the main files still live on the hard-drive array. 
 This guide includes systems with M.2 NVMe or 2.5-inch SSD storage that can be used as the primary pool. 
 3. A diskless price below $500 
 The comparison uses the chassis price before SSDs, taxes, and shipping. 
 We also distinguish between a normal listed price and a short promotional price. A product that occasionally drops below $500 may be a good deal, but it should not be treated as a consistently available sub-$500 option. 
 Candidate comparison 
 Model Price checked Network Main storage options Result 
 LincStation N2 $405 direct 1× 10GbE RJ45 4× M.2 NVMe + 2× 2.5-inch SATA Meets all three criteria 
 TerraMaster F8 SSD $659.99 direct 1× 10GBASE-T 8× M.2 NVMe Above the $500 limit 
 TerraMaster F4 SSD Check current retailer price 1× 5GbE RJ45 4× M.2 NVMe Does not meet the 10GbE requirement 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Varies by retailer 2× 2.5GbE 4× SATA + 2× M.2 No single 10GbE port; HDD-primary design 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus $619.99 direct 1× 10GbE + 1× 2.5GbE 4× SATA + 2× M.2 Above $500 and primarily designed around SATA bays 
 UniFi UNAS Pro $499 direct 1× 10G SFP+ 7× 2.5/3.5-inch SATA Meets the price and network checks, but is not an all-flash design 
 TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus $719.99 direct 1× 10GBASE-T 8× M.2 NVMe Above the $500 limit 
 AOOSTAR WTR Max i5-1235U $559 barebone Dual 10G SFP+ + dual 2.5GbE 6× SATA + 5× M.2 Above $500 before memory and software 
 The table is not a ranking of overall product quality. It only shows whether each model meets the narrow definition used in this article. 
 A hard-drive NAS may be the better choice for a 40TB archive. A more expensive eight-slot SSD NAS may be the better choice for a growing production team. The right purchase depends on the workload, not simply on which row passes the most filters. 
 The model that clearly fits the requirement 
 LincStation N2 
 The LincStation N2 combines the following hardware in a compact diskless system: 
 Intel N100 processor with four cores and four threads 
 16GB LPDDR5 memory 
 128GB eMMC system storage 
 One 10GbE RJ45 port 
 Four M.2 2280 NVMe slots 
 Two 2.5-inch SATA SSD bays 
 Unraid preinstalled with a Starter license 
 At the time of checking, the LincPlus store listed the diskless N2 at $405 . 
 The combination is aimed at home labs, creators, media servers, Docker applications, backups, and users who want a compact SSD NAS without adding a separate 10GbE card. 
 Where the N2 fits well 
 The N2 is a practical option for: 
 Large-file transfers from one or a few workstations 
 Video and photo project storage 
 Docker containers and self-hosted services 
 Jellyfin, Plex, Immich, and home-server applications 
 Quiet desktop or shelf installations 
 Users who already plan to use Unraid 
 Its six storage positions also allow more flexibility than a four-slot M.2-only design. A user could build an NVMe pool, use the two SATA bays for additional SSD capacity, or separate application data from bulk storage. 
 Where the N2 has limits 
 The Intel N100 is an efficient entry-level processor, not a workstation-class CPU. 
 It is well suited to file services and lightweight containers, but users planning several continuously active virtual machines, heavy software compilation, or demanding multi-user compute workloads should consider a higher-core platform. 
 Compact Intel N100 systems also have a limited PCIe lane budget. Installing four NVMe drives does not mean every drive can operate at its maximum advertised speed at the same time. For a typical single-client 10GbE workload, that may not be a practical problem. For several users hitting different drives simultaneously, platform bandwidth matters more. 
 The closest alternatives 
 TerraMaster F8 SSD 
 The F8 SSD provides eight M.2 NVMe slots and a 10GBASE-T connection. Its main advantage is capacity expansion: users can add more M.2 drives without moving to an external enclosure. 
 The official US store listed it at $659.99 when checked, placing it outside this article’s budget. Retailer promotions may occasionally narrow the gap, so it is worth comparing current prices before ordering. 
 The eight M.2 slots use PCIe 3.0 ×1 connections per drive. That is enough to build an aggregate pool capable of using a 10GbE connection, but it is not the same as giving every SSD a full-width NVMe link. 
 TerraMaster F4 SSD 
 The F4 SSD is a compact four-slot all-flash NAS, but its published network interface is 5GbE , not 10GbE. 
 That does not make it a poor product. For many home users, 5GbE provides more than enough bandwidth with lower networking costs. It simply does not meet the true 10GbE definition used here. 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 
 The DXP4800 Plus includes a real 10GbE port and a capable Intel Pentium Gold 8505 processor. Its four main bays are designed for SATA hard drives or SSDs, with two additional M.2 slots. 
 At $619.99 on the official US store when checked, it exceeds the $500 limit. It is also better described as a flexible hybrid NAS than a purpose-built compact all-flash system. 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 
 The UNAS Pro costs $499 and includes a 10G SFP+ connection, so it meets two of the three checks. 
 Its seven bays are designed for 2.5-inch or 3.5-inch SATA drives. It is a strong fit for rack-mounted shared storage, particularly in an existing UniFi environment, but it is not an M.2 all-flash NAS. 
 AOOSTAR WTR Max 
 The Intel WTR Max starts at $559 and offers dual 10G SFP+, dual 2.5GbE, six SATA positions, and five M.2 slots. 
 It offers considerably more expansion than the systems below $500, but the entry price is for a barebone configuration. Memory, storage, and the operating system must be added separately. 
 The chassis is only part of the budget 
 A $405 or $499 NAS is not a complete all-flash system. The SSDs, networking equipment, and client hardware can easily account for most of the final cost. 
 Before choosing the enclosure, calculate the full build. 
 1. SSDs 
 Every system in this comparison is diskless. 
 The final SSD cost depends on: 
 Capacity per drive 
 TLC or QLC NAND 
 Endurance rating 
 Whether the drive includes DRAM 
 Thermal design 
 Warranty 
 Current promotions 
 For many buyers, starting with two larger SSDs is more practical than filling every slot with smaller drives. It reduces the initial cost and leaves space for later expansion. 
 The correct layout depends on whether the priority is capacity, redundancy, or performance. RAID and mirrored pools protect against a drive failure, but they are not a substitute for a separate backup. 
 2. The 10GbE connection 
 There are two common ways to connect a 10GbE NAS. 
 Through a switch 
 A 10GbE switch is useful when several computers need high-speed access. 
 A typical setup may require: 
 A 10GbE switch 
 A compatible network card for each workstation 
 DAC cables, Cat6a cables, or transceivers 
 Correct SFP+ or 10GBASE-T compatibility 
 This is the more flexible option, but it adds cost, power consumption, heat, and configuration work. 
 Directly to one workstation 
 When only one computer needs the full 10GbE connection, direct attachment is often the simplest option. 
 Connect the NAS directly to the workstation with a compatible cable, then assign both 10GbE interfaces static addresses on a separate subnet. The normal network connection can continue to handle internet access and other devices. 
 For example: 
 Workstation 10GbE interface: 10.0.10.1 
 NAS 10GbE interface: 10.0.10.2 
 Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0 
 No gateway or DNS on the direct 10GbE interfaces 
 This avoids buying a switch solely for one fast client. 
 3. Client-side networking 
 The computer also needs a 10GbE interface. 
 Some workstations and higher-end motherboards include one. Many do not. Before ordering the NAS, check whether the client needs: 
 A PCIe 10GbE network card 
 A Thunderbolt-to-10GbE adapter 
 An SFP+ card 
 A 10GBASE-T card 
 Updated drivers 
 The NAS cannot deliver 10GbE performance through a 1GbE or 2.5GbE client port. 
 4. The operating system 
 Operating-system cost depends on the platform. 
 TrueNAS and OpenMediaVault are available without a license fee. Unraid uses paid licenses. The current Unraid lineup includes Starter, Unleashed, and Lifetime options, with different storage-device and update terms. 
 The LincStation N2 includes an Unraid Starter license, which is useful for buyers who already prefer Unraid. Buyers who intend to install another operating system should evaluate the hardware independently of the bundled license. 
 Three realistic build approaches 
 Exact SSD prices change frequently, so the examples below focus on configuration rather than claiming a fixed all-in total. 
 Entry build 
 LincStation N2 
 Two NVMe SSDs 
 Direct 10GbE connection to one workstation 
 Existing home network used for internet and other devices 
 This is the lowest-cost practical route for one user who wants fast local project storage and room to expand. 
 Balanced build 
 LincStation N2 
 Four NVMe SSDs 
 A redundant or parity-protected storage layout 
 A 10GbE network card for the workstation 
 Direct connection or a small 10GbE switch 
 This configuration suits creators, home labs, and users running several services from the same NAS. 
 Expansion-focused build 
 An eight-slot system such as the TerraMaster F8 SSD or F8 SSD Plus 
 Four SSDs initially, with empty slots reserved for growth 
 A multi-client 10GbE switch 
 A higher-core CPU if virtual machines are important 
 This costs more upfront, but reduces the chance of replacing the enclosure when the storage pool grows. 
 When 10GbE makes a real difference 
 10GbE is most useful when the workload can sustain large sequential transfers. 
 Good examples include: 
 Editing high-bitrate video directly from the NAS 
 Moving large video masters or disk images 
 Working with large photography catalogs 
 Hosting virtual-machine disks over the network 
 Copying 100GB or larger datasets during the working day 
 Supporting several active clients on an SSD pool 
 A well-configured 10GbE connection can be several times faster than gigabit Ethernet for these tasks. Actual performance still depends on the storage layout, protocol, client hardware, filesystem, cooling, and network configuration. 
 When 2.5GbE is enough 
 Many home NAS workloads do not need 10GbE. 
 A 2.5GbE connection is usually sufficient for: 
 Jellyfin or Plex streaming 
 Phone and computer backups 
 General document sharing 
 Photo backup 
 A small hard-drive array 
 Overnight backup jobs 
 One or two home users 
 A typical 4K Blu-ray remux uses only a small fraction of a gigabit link. Faster storage and networking do not improve video quality, and they do not solve client compatibility, Wi-Fi congestion, or transcoding limitations. 
 For these workloads, 2.5GbE usually offers a better balance of cost, heat, and simplicity. 
 Why a 10GbE NAS may not reach 10GbE speed 
 A 10GbE port does not guarantee 1GB/s file transfers. 
 Common limits include: 
 Storage-pool performance 
 One slow SATA SSD, an inefficient parity layout, or a pool performing background work may limit transfers. 
 Small files 
 Thousands of small files create metadata and open-and-close overhead. They rarely transfer at the same rate as one large video file. 
 SSD thermal throttling 
 NVMe drives in a compact enclosure can become hot during sustained writes. Once a controller reaches its thermal limit, performance may drop until the drive cools. 
 Use suitable thermal pads or heatsinks where supported, maintain airflow, and check drive temperatures during long transfers. 
 Network configuration 
 Possible causes include: 
 Incorrect drivers 
 Receive Side Scaling disabled 
 A damaged or unsuitable cable 
 Mismatched MTU settings 
 A slow transceiver 
 An older PCIe slot limiting the client network card 
 Start troubleshooting with one large file. That separates network and storage throughput from small-file overhead. 
 Which type of buyer should choose each system? 
 Creator working directly from the NAS 
 Prioritize: 
 True 10GbE 
 SSD primary storage 
 Reliable cooling 
 A direct connection or low-latency switch 
 Enough capacity for active projects 
 The LincStation N2 is a cost-effective option for one or a few users. An eight-slot system may be a better long-term choice when project capacity is expected to grow quickly. 
 Home lab and container user 
 Prioritize: 
 Memory 
 Docker support 
 Low idle power 
 Quiet operation 
 Flexible storage pools 
 Easy backup of application data 
 The N2’s Intel N100 and included Unraid license are well matched to file services and lightweight containers. Heavy virtual-machine users should choose a higher-core platform. 
 Small business with several active users 
 Prioritize: 
 CPU headroom 
 Memory expansion 
 Multi-client network design 
 Backup and recovery 
 Warranty and support 
 Storage expansion 
 A sub-$500 N100 or N95 system can work for file sharing, but a growing business may benefit from a more powerful processor and additional drive positions. 
 Large media archive 
 Prioritize cost per terabyte rather than flash performance. 
 For tens of terabytes of movies and backups, a hard-drive NAS with NVMe used for applications, metadata, or cache is usually more economical than an all-flash build. 
 Buying checklist 
 Before placing an order, confirm the following: 
 Is the network port really 10GbE? 
 Check the manufacturer’s specification page rather than relying on a search-result title. 
 Can SSDs be used as the primary storage pool? 
 Do not assume M.2 slots are intended for primary data; some systems limit them to cache. 
 Does the listed price include drives? 
 Most NAS products are sold diskless. 
 How are the M.2 slots connected? 
 The number of slots does not reveal the PCIe bandwidth available to each drive. 
 Does the workstation have 10GbE? 
 Add the cost of a network card or adapter when necessary. 
 Do you need a switch? 
 One fast workstation can often use a direct connection. 
 What operating system will you use? 
 Include license costs and check hardware compatibility. 
 How will you back up the NAS? 
 RAID, parity, and mirrors do not protect against accidental deletion, malware, theft, or enclosure failure. 
 Can the enclosure cool the selected SSDs? 
 Check heatsink clearance, thermal-pad support, and sustained-load temperatures. 
 Was the price checked recently? 
 NAS and SSD promotions change often. 
 FAQ 
 Is there a true 10GbE all-flash NAS under $500? 
 Yes, but the selection is limited. Among the widely available US models verified for this guide, the LincStation N2 met all three criteria at its listed price. 
 Availability and pricing change, so check current product pages before ordering. 
 Do I need a 10GbE switch? 
 Not necessarily. 
 A switch is useful when several computers need high-speed access. For one workstation, a direct connection between the NAS and computer is often simpler and less expensive. 
 Is 10GbE worth it for a home NAS? 
 It depends on the workload. 
 10GbE is useful for large files, direct video editing, virtual-machine storage, and active SSD-based workflows. It is usually unnecessary for media streaming, ordinary backups, and general home file sharing. 
 Why is my 10GbE NAS only transferring at 300MB/s? 
 Possible causes include the storage pool, small files, SSD thermal throttling, network-card drivers, cable quality, MTU mismatch, or a client-side PCIe limitation. 
 Test with one large file first, then monitor disk temperature, CPU use, and network utilization. 
 Do the NAS units include SSDs? 
 No. The systems discussed here are sold diskless unless a specific bundle says otherwise. 
 Is an all-flash NAS better than an HDD NAS? 
 Not for every workload. 
 All-flash systems are compact, quiet, responsive, and strong at random I/O. Hard drives remain more economical for large media archives and backup capacity. A hybrid design is often the most practical option. 
 Final recommendation 
 The LincStation N2 is a strong fit for buyers looking for a compact SSD NAS with true 10GbE, six storage positions, and Unraid included at a sub-$500 chassis price. 
 It is not the right choice for every buyer. Users who need eight M.2 slots should compare the TerraMaster F8 SSD range. Users building a large rack-mounted archive may be better served by the UniFi UNAS Pro or another hard-drive platform. Users running several demanding virtual machines should consider a system with more CPU cores and expandable memory. 
 The useful question is not simply, “Which NAS has 10GbE?” 
 It is: 
 Will your storage pool, workstation, workload, and budget make meaningful use of it?

Best NAS for Homelab (2026): UGREEN vs TerraMaster vs Synology Skip to main content 
 This isn’t a generic “best NAS” list. Those exist, and PCMag writes them better than I can. This is for homelab people: you want a box that stores files and runs Docker containers, hosts a VM or two, feeds Plex/Jellyfin transcoding, and talks fast to your Proxmox cluster over NFS or iSCSI. That narrows the field to NAS units with real CPUs, enough RAM headroom, and 2.5GbE or better networking.
 Affiliate disclosure
 Some links on this page are affiliate links. If you buy through them, I earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.
 How I picked these
 I started with every NAS on Amazon shipping an x86 CPU, 8GB+ RAM (or an upgrade slot), at least one M.2 NVMe bay, and 2.5GbE networking, then cut anything above $1,300 diskless. ARM-only units are out (most VM images and a chunk of container images won’t run), and so are boxes with soldered, non-upgradable RAM under 8GB.
 What’s left is a short list. I evaluated each on four things: CPU performance per dollar, RAM ceiling, out-of-box networking speed, and whether the OS lets you run Docker and VMs without hacks. I also weighed the option of skipping a NAS entirely and building a mini PC + DAS; for some homelabs that’s the better call.

 What actually matters for a Docker/Proxmox NAS
 RAM headroom. Docker containers and a couple of VMs eat RAM faster than CPU. 8GB is the floor; 32GB is comfortable. Non-upgradable RAM (looking at you, soldered models) is a hard stop.
 An NVMe slot for apps. Spinning disks are for bulk storage. Container volumes, databases, and VM disks belong on the M.2 slots every pick here includes.
 2.5GbE minimum. Containers serving your LAN and Proxmox nodes pulling VM disks over NFS saturate 1GbE instantly. 10GbE future-proofs the link to your main server and the switch everything hangs off.
 x86 CPU. ARM NAS units are cheaper but rule out most VM images and some container images. Every pick below is x86.
 Transcoding. If Jellyfin/Plex lives on the NAS, you want Intel QuickSync, which the Synology’s Ryzen doesn’t have. If it doesn’t have to live on the NAS, a small Intel box handles it: see the best mini PC for Plex and Jellyfin .
 1. UGREEN DXP2800: the $340 entry point
 UGREEN DXP2800 
 $339.99 on Oct 23 (list $389.99) · 4.6★, 951 ratings · shipped by Amazon, sold by UGREEN · it was the #1 Best Seller in NAS devices when I first checked on Sep 21
 Two bays, Intel N100, 8GB DDR5, a single 2.5GbE port, and two M.2 NVMe slots. The NVMe slots matter more than the bays for this audience: put your container volumes and app databases on NVMe and let the HDDs be pure bulk storage. UGOS supports Docker and VMs, so the whole home-server container stack runs on it.
 Where it fits: a first NAS, a Plex/Jellyfin box for a small library, or a dedicated backup target for your Proxmox cluster (a cheap NAS doing one job well is a legitimate architecture). Where it doesn’t: heavy VM duty or anything needing more than ~80TB of raw capacity (two bays × 24TB NAS drives, RAID 1). Two bays also means RAID 1 or nothing, so plan your redundancy accordingly.

 2. UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: best hardware per dollar
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus 
 $656.99 on Oct 23 (list $729.99) · 4.6★, 631 ratings · shipped by Amazon, sold by UGREEN
 The spec sheet reads like it was designed by r/homelab: Pentium Gold 8505, 10GbE + 2.5GbE onboard, 4 SATA bays + 2 M.2 NVMe slots, DDR5 expandable to 64GB, and hardware transcoding including AV1 decode. Nothing else near $650 ships 10GbE. That’s the gap.
 UGOS (UGREEN’s OS) has Docker and VM support built in, and UGREEN officially lets you install TrueNAS, Unraid, or Proxmox instead, with no warranty games. The trade-off: UGOS is functional and improving, but it’s younger and rougher than Synology’s DSM. If you plan to run your own OS anyway, that doesn’t matter.

 3. TerraMaster F4-424 Pro: the compute king
 TerraMaster F4-424 Pro 
 $730.99 (list $859.99) · 4.2★, 62 reviews
 The i3-N305 gives you 8 cores and 8 threads (the strongest CPU here) plus 32GB of DDR5 out of the box . For Docker-heavy workloads that’s the most capable machine in this list: the RAM you actually need is already installed.
 The catch is TOS, TerraMaster’s operating system. It works (Docker support exists) but it’s the weakest software of the three, and TerraMaster had documented security issues in 2022–2023: deadbolt ransomware targeted TOS vulnerabilities, and patches were slow. The community’s fix is well-worn: buy the hardware, flash TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid , and never boot TOS. If that plan appeals to you, this is your box. If you want a turnkey appliance you’ll never SSH into, look at the Synology or UGREEN instead.

 4. Synology DS925+: the software king, with asterisks
 Synology DS925+ 
 $742.62 (list $889.99) · 4.2★, 156 reviews · Amazon’s Choice
 DSM is still the best NAS software by a mile: Active Backup, Photos, Drive, Surveillance Station, and a container manager that just works. If the point of the NAS is to be a reliable appliance you’ll forget about for five years, this is the safe pick.
 The asterisks are real, though. The Ryzen V1500B is a 4-core chip with no integrated GPU, so no hardware transcoding , which rules it out as a Jellyfin box for remote clients. It ships with 4GB of RAM you’ll want to upgrade immediately. And the DS925+ generation restricts storage to Synology’s drive compatibility list, which pushed a chunk of the community toward third-party NAS brands this year. Docker containers run fine in Container Manager; for Proxmox it’s a storage target, not a compute node.

 5. UGREEN DXP6800 Pro: the small-server replacement
 UGREEN DXP6800 Pro 
 $1,049.99 on Oct 23 (list $1,209.99) · 4.5★, 90 ratings · shipped by Amazon, sold by UGREEN
 The premium end of the range, and it earns it: a 10-core/12-thread i5-1235U, two 10GbE ports (aggregable to 20G), two Thunderbolt 4 ports for direct-attach editing, a built-in 128GB SSD for the OS, 6 SATA bays plus 2 M.2 NVMe for up to 208TB, and RAID 0/1/5/6/10. That’s the spec sheet of a small tower server, not an appliance. It can host the whole container stack plus several VMs while serving storage to a Proxmox cluster over 10GbE.
 The audience here is narrower: homelabbers consolidating into one “do-everything” box, or small offices. At $1,050 diskless, price it against a mini PC + DAS build first. The mini PC gets you more compute for less money. The 6800 Pro gets you six hot-swap bays in one box with a 3-year warranty.

 Drives are the expensive half of a NAS right now. Every new-condition hard drive listing I checked on Oct 23 was from a third-party seller, and the cheapest price per TB was a renewed enterprise drive. Three rules before the table:
 CMR only. SMR drives (plain WD Red, most desktop drives) take far longer to rebuild a RAID array or resilver a ZFS pool, and a slow rebuild is when a second drive fails. Seagate IronWolf and IronWolf Pro, WD Red Plus and Red Pro, and Toshiba N300 are CMR lines.
 Buy for the capacity you’ll need in three years. Bays are the scarce resource, not dollars per TB.

Four of them in RAID 5 on the DXP4800 Plus give you 36TB usable for about $1,800. For container volumes and VM disks, put an NVMe drive in the M.2 slots and keep the hard drives for bulk storage.
 Also worth knowing
 UGREEN DXP480T Plus (~$999): the all-flash sibling. 4x NVMe bays, no SATA, 10GbE. If your homelab data fits in ~16TB of SSD (and you value silence over raw capacity), it’s a clean option. The lack of SATA bays means no cheap bulk storage, though. Every TB costs flash prices.
 QNAP TS-464: a year ago this was a contender. The Intel N5095 is showing its age against the N305 and Pentium Gold 8505 in the picks above, QNAP’s software has had its own security troubles, and the price hasn’t dropped to match. I’d skip it this cycle.
 Or skip the NAS: mini PC + DAS
 Before buying a NAS at all, price the alternative: an N150 mini PC running Proxmox or plain Docker, plus a USB DAS enclosure for the bulk disks. On Oct 23 that was a Beelink EQ14 at $369 (16GB, dual 2.5GbE; more options in the home server mini PC guide ) and a TerraMaster D4-320 at $170.99 (4 bays over 10Gbps USB-C, 4.2★ from 395 ratings). That’s about $540 diskless, against $657 for the DXP4800 Plus.

 If you already run a Proxmox mini PC or plan to, a NAS appliance is mostly redundant. Attach storage to the cluster and be done. Buy the NAS when you want storage to be a separate, boring, always-on appliance that survives your cluster experiments.
 One caveat with the DAS route: a USB enclosure puts a USB bridge between the disks and the OS. ZFS and mdadm work on it, but a flaky bridge shows up as disks dropping out of the pool. On day one, check that SMART data comes through ( smartctl -a /dev/sdX ) and leave the pool under load for a few hours before you trust it with data.
 If I were buying today
 Under $400: The DXP2800 . It runs Docker and VMs, the N100 sips power, and you can always add a second NAS later if you outgrow two bays.
 Best overall for homelab: The DXP4800 Plus . 10GbE at $657 is a hardware gap nobody else closes, and the 64GB RAM ceiling means you won’t hit a wall.
 Most compute for the money: The F4-424 Pro , but only if you’re flashing your own OS. The i3-N305 + 32GB out of the box is hard to beat if you never plan to touch TOS.
 Best appliance experience: The DS925+ . Accept no transcoding and the drive whitelist, and you get software that genuinely works for five years with minimal attention.
 Money no object, one box: The DXP6800 Pro . i5, dual 10GbE, six bays, TB4. It replaces a small server.
 And whichever you buy, put it on a UPS. A CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the $240 insurance that keeps a hard power cut from corrupting your array. If the NAS sits in a rack, the best rack mount UPS guide covers 1U and 2U units. More on that and the rest of the homelab stack in my Black Friday deals tracker and the Docker containers guide .
 FAQ
 What is the best NAS for a homelab in 2026? For most homelabs, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus: $656.99 on Oct 23, 10GbE plus 2.5GbE, 4 bays plus 2 NVMe slots, RAM up to 64GB, and official support for running TrueNAS, Unraid or Proxmox instead of UGOS. Under $400, the DXP2800. If you want the best software and don’t need hardware transcoding, the Synology DS925+.
 Which hard drives should I put in a NAS? CMR NAS drives: Seagate IronWolf or IronWolf Pro, WD Red Plus or Red Pro, Toshiba N300. Avoid SMR drives in any RAID or ZFS pool. On Oct 23 the best new-drive value I found was the Seagate IronWolf 12TB at $449.99 ($37.50 per TB) from a third-party seller. A renewed Exos X24 was cheaper per TB, with a refurbisher warranty instead of Seagate’s.
 Can these NAS units run Docker containers directly? Yes. All three support Docker natively (UGREEN and Synology have container managers in their OS; TerraMaster supports Docker in TOS). For heavier VM workloads, the UGREEN and TerraMaster hardware handles it; the Synology’s 4GB of base RAM needs an upgrade first.
 Do I need 10GbE for a homelab NAS? Not strictly. 2.5GbE saturates HDDs fine (~280MB/s). 10GbE matters when you add NVMe pools, run VM disks over NFS/iSCSI, or have multiple clients hitting the NAS at once. The DXP4800 Plus having it at $657 removes the dilemma.
 What's the Synology drive whitelist issue? The DS925+ generation only supports drives on Synology’s compatibility list, which favors Synology-branded and enterprise drives and excludes many popular WD/Seagate models. It’s the main reason long-time Synology users have been defecting to UGREEN and DIY builds.
 NAS or just a big USB drive on my mini PC? A DAS enclosure on a mini PC is cheaper and simpler for single-server setups. Buy the NAS when you want RAID management, snapshots, and backups handled by software designed for it, or when storage needs to stay up while your compute boxes get experimented on.
 How much RAM do I need for Docker on a NAS? 8GB runs a handful of containers. If you’re adding Immich, a Plex instance, a couple of databases, and maybe a Home Assistant VM, 32GB is where it stops being tight. That’s why the F4-424 Pro shipping with 32GB matters.

NAS Price Tracker: Synology, QNAP & More | Brandon Sheley 
 Homelab 
 NAS Enclosure Price Tracker
 Synology, QNAP, TerraMaster, ASUSTOR & UGREEN: Bare, Drive-Less Enclosures
 The enclosure and the drives are two separate purchases, and buying them separately is almost always the better value. You pick the exact capacity you want instead of paying a premium for a pre-populated bundle. This tracks current $/bay pricing on bare, drive-less enclosures across the five brands homelabbers and data hoarders actually buy, from 2-bay desktop units up through 8-bay rackmount chassis. Pair it with my disk price tracker to source the drives, and if your unit does 2.5G or 10G, check my switch price tracker too, since a NAS is only as fast as the port it's plugged into.
 As of Nov 3, 2026: 23 working listings (for-parts and as-is excluded). Best value $125/bay, median $185/bay. Price history logged since Oct 11, 2026 (497 listing-days). Live from eBay listings. How this data is collected .
 Price Alert 
 Never miss a price drop 
 One click to confirm, one click to unsubscribe — no account needed.
 Sizing: How Many Bays Do You Actually Need
 Bay count is the number that matters most when comparing NAS enclosures across brands, which is why this page sorts by $/bay rather than raw price. It's the closest thing to an apples-to-apples unit of expansion headroom, since a cheap 2-bay unit and a pricier 8-bay unit can have wildly different value depending on what you need to store.
 2 bays covers basic mirrored redundancy (RAID1) with no room to grow. 4 bays is the sweet spot for most homelabbers, enough for single-parity redundancy (RAID5/SHR) with real usable capacity and a spare slot for expansion. 5-8 bays starts to matter once you're seriously data hoarding, where dual-parity redundancy (RAID6/SHR-2) protects against a second drive failing mid-rebuild, which becomes a real risk once you're running larger, older drives.
 The Five Brands on This Page
 Synology
 The most polished, locked-down software ecosystem (DSM) with the broadest app support. It comes at a real price premium, and it's grown pickier about non-Synology drives on newer models.
 QNAP
 More raw hardware and features per dollar than Synology, but has had more publicized security vulnerabilities, so stay current on firmware updates.
 TerraMaster
 Budget-friendly hardware with a smaller software ecosystem, which appeals most to people planning to run TrueNAS or Unraid instead of the stock firmware.
 ASUSTOR
 Similar positioning to TerraMaster: competitive hardware specs at a lower price than Synology/QNAP, with a smaller but still active app ecosystem.
 UGREEN
 The newest of the five, with aggressive hardware per dollar (10GbE and even Thunderbolt 4 on some models), but its UGOS Pro software is younger and thinner than the rest, so it's a good fit if you plan to run TrueNAS or Unraid anyway.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Should I buy a bare NAS enclosure or one bundled with drives?
 Buying bare and sourcing your own drives, often from a dedicated drive tracker rather than the NAS vendor, is usually cheaper and lets you pick the exact capacity and drive model you want. A bundled unit can be a reasonable convenience if you'd rather not manually test and burn in drives yourself, but you'll typically pay a premium for that.
 How many drive bays do I actually need?
 2 bays gets you basic mirrored redundancy with no room to grow. 4 bays is the sweet spot for most homelabbers: enough for RAID5/SHR with real capacity and a spare slot. 5-8 bays starts to matter for serious data hoarding, where dual-parity redundancy (RAID6/SHR-2) protects against a second drive failing during a rebuild.
 Synology vs QNAP vs TerraMaster vs ASUSTOR vs UGREEN: What's the Real Difference?
 Synology has the most polished, locked-down software ecosystem (DSM) with broad app support, but costs more and has grown more restrictive about non-Synology-branded drives on newer models. QNAP offers more raw hardware per dollar and a deeper feature set, but has had more publicized security vulnerabilities, so timely firmware updates matter. TerraMaster and ASUSTOR are the budget-friendlier options with smaller software ecosystems, which appeals most to people planning to run their own OS instead of the stock firmware. UGREEN is the newest entrant, and it shows: aggressive hardware for the price (10GbE and even Thunderbolt 4 show up at lower price points than the competition), but its UGOS Pro software is younger and thinner than the other four, so it appeals most to buyers who plan to run TrueNAS or Unraid anyway.
 Can I run TrueNAS or Unraid on one of these instead of the stock OS?
 Many x86-based NAS enclosures (most QNAP, TerraMaster, ASUSTOR, and UGREEN units, and some Synology Plus-series models) can run TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid instead of, or alongside, the stock firmware. UGREEN's NASync line is a standard x86 machine under the hood and is explicitly marketed as friendly to this. Compatibility varies model to model though, especially for vendor-specific hardware like front-panel LED and LCD control. Search your exact model number plus "TrueNAS" or "Unraid" to see what other owners ran into.
 Should I worry about buying a used NAS enclosure?
 It's a relatively low-risk used purchase. The parts that actually wear out in a NAS (fans and the power supply) are common and usually inexpensive to replace, and the drive bay backplane rarely fails since it sees far less stress than the drives themselves. Just make sure all the drive trays are included: they're often proprietary to the model and hard to track down separately if any are missing. Also confirm the seller actually wiped the drives, since a used NAS' data destruction is on the previous owner, not you. If you're the one retiring an old NAS or its drives instead, see E-Waste Recycling for secure destruction and responsible disposal in Topeka and Shawnee County.
 What's the power draw like on a NAS enclosure?
 By the makers' own spec sheets, a 4-bay NAS draws about 35-42W with its drives active and 11-22W with them spun down, a 2-bay about 12-16W active, and 5- to 8-bay units about 43-54W. Running 24/7 at 40W costs about $65 a year at the U.S. average rate.
